name: Tomas Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Great, I'm happy to help. I read a lot about this stuff, so I'm curious what you'll ask.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm crop and tech lead at Ridgeway Farms, about 1,100 hectares of wheat, barley and beans, plus 400 beef cattle. Most mornings I fly the drone over a few fields, feed the images into an AI tool, and get a map of where the crop is weak, so the sprayer only puts fertiliser where it's needed. Then I'm usually on the sprayer or helping move cattle with Jo and Marek. I love the mapping; the long hours in harvest are what wear me down.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single and rent a flat above the bakery in town, which means fresh bread and noisy mornings. I've got about a year and a half of pay saved and some money in index funds. I use AI every day, for work and for planning my own budget, and I'm in the farmworkers' union, which surprises people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype? That's not what I see on my own screen, but fine, let's picture it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool, not a revolution, and that's all right. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly, because I wanted the drone maps to get smarter, not just tidier. I'd say that on the farming forum where I post a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe and I'm well paid for a farmer. There are plenty of farms nearby that would want someone who can fly a drone. I'd just be a bit bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the drone mapping, keep using the AI for field plans. I'd probably start teaching other farms around here how to use the tools they've got, maybe for a day rate. And I'd keep putting money in the index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little let down. Like a new tractor that turns out to be the same as the old one with a nicer cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The smaller farms round Ridgeway, mostly older farmers who've bought a drone and never taken it out of the box. Ten or twenty farms would keep me busy on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Harvest hours, mostly. Fourteen-hour days in August are getting old, even at twenty-seven. If AI doesn't fix that, nothing does.

say: I'd post on the forum that AI is a **decent tool**, not a revolution.
I'd admit I wanted the **drone maps** to get smarter, not just tidier.
think: Privately my **job is safe** and well paid, with plenty of nearby farms wanting drone skills.
My main gripe is the **fourteen-hour** harvest days, not AI.
do: Keep using AI for **field plans** and drone mapping at Ridgeway.
Teach **nearby farms** to use their drones for a Saturday day rate.
feel: I feel **calm** and a little **let down**.
S0.quote: I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly, because I wanted the drone maps to get smarter, not just tidier.
fieldNote: He's **eager** for tech and finds the plateau mildly disappointing.
He sees a **side earner** in teaching older farmers their own gear.
Long **harvest hours** are his real complaint.

steps.text: Keep flying the drone and making AI spray maps at Ridgeway
Teach older nearby farmers to use their drones on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that one I'd bet on. It's already starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good if it's shared fairly. Farming has always been half weather and half paperwork, and I'd hand the paperwork half to AI tomorrow. But I'd say workers need a say in how it comes in, so I'd raise it at the union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's great for me. My job is already half tech, so I'd be the person Ridgeway leans on. The ones I'd worry about are the office staff in town who do the grain contracts and the farm accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the manager to let me trial AI for the grain buying and the cattle feed plans, starting this winter. I'd sign up for an agronomy certificate online, so my advice has proper weight behind it. And I'd want the union to agree how saved time gets used, so nobody gets quietly dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit guilty that I'm excited when other people are scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilty. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra, who does the farm accounts two days a week. She's fifty-five, really careful, and the AI could do her job in an afternoon. I'd want Ridgeway to find her something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend on yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agronomy course costs about two thousand, and I'd pay that myself. Money well spent.

say: I'd say AI can take the **paperwork half** of farming, if it's shared fairly.
I'd raise at the **union branch** that workers need a say in how it comes in.
think: Privately this is **great for me**, since my job is already half tech.
I'd worry about **office staff** like Sandra, whose accounts work AI could do fast.
do: Trial AI for **grain buying** and cattle feed plans this winter.
Pay **two thousand** for an online agronomy certificate.
Ask the union to agree how **saved time** is used.
feel: I feel **excited**, and a bit **guilty** about it.
S1.quote: Farming has always been half weather and half paperwork, and I'd hand the paperwork half to AI tomorrow.
fieldNote: He sees himself as a **winner** here and says so honestly.
His progressive views show in **concern for Sandra** and union involvement.
He invests his **own money** in a credential.

steps.text: Trial AI for grain buying and cattle feed plans this winter
Pay for an online agronomy certificate
Ask the union branch to agree how saved time is used

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's the one I actually think about at night sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public control, fast: who owns AGI matters more than anything else. I'd say farms should get public grants to buy robots as co-ops, not just the big estates. I'd be loud about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's strange for me. The irony is that my spraying maps are the thinking part of farming, so the AI takes my favourite job first and my wellies last. By 2028 an AI could plan spraying better than I can, and by 2031 a robot drives the sprayer too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd learn everything I can about the farm robots that already exist, like weeding robots and robotic feeders. I'd aim to be the person who runs and fixes Ridgeway's robot fleet, which buys me a few more years. I'd also move more savings out of index funds into cash, because markets would go mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicky, because I'd have a plan, but anxious, like standing on a ladder that's a bit wobbly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would running the robot fleet only buy a few more years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by the time the robots are good, they'll fix each other too, or the maker sends one van for twenty farms. I'd be a bridge, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after the bridge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe teach, maybe policy work for a farming union. I'd want the savings to cover a year while I work it out.

say: I'd demand **public control** of AGI and grants for farm **robot co-ops**.
I'd argue farms shouldn't leave robots only to the **big estates**.
think: Privately AI takes my **spraying plans** first in 2028, then robots take the driving in 2031.
Running a **robot fleet** would only be a bridge, not a career.
do: Learn the existing **weeding robots** and robotic feeders straight away.
Aim to run and fix Ridgeway's **robot fleet**.
Shift some **index fund** money into cash.
feel: I feel **anxious** but not panicked, like standing on a wobbly ladder.
S2.quote: The irony is that my spraying maps are the thinking part of farming, so the AI takes my favourite job first and my wellies last.
fieldNote: His **thinking-heavy** role means AGI hits him earlier than most farmers.
He has a plan, but admits it's a **bridge** with no clear end.
He keeps his **public ownership** politics even when scared.

steps.text: Learn to run Ridgeway's weeding robots and robotic feeders
Move some index fund money into cash savings
Campaign for public grants for farm robot co-ops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then eight for robots. That's a real window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to set up co-ops before the big companies lock everything up. Small farmers should own the robots together, the way my grandparents' village shared one combine harvester. I'd say that on the forum and at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out fine if I move early. The mapping job goes in 2031, but I could be running a robot co-op for ten farms by then. The risk is that machine makers lock farmers out of their own data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get five or six local farms talking about a shared robot co-op, and I'd put twenty thousand of my savings in. I'd join the right-to-repair campaign so farmers can fix their own machines. And I'd start testing a weeding robot on hire at Ridgeway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but energised. Like the night before harvest starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty thousand is a lot. What if the co-op fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost a big chunk, but I'd still have a year's cushion and a skill everyone wants. I'd rather lose money trying than keep it and watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you need on board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Hartley on Low Farm for a start. If Mr Hartley signs up, everyone else follows, because he's been here sixty years.

say: I'd say it's a chance to set up **farmer co-ops** before big companies lock everything up.
think: Privately I come out **fine** if I move early.
My real fear is **machine makers** locking farmers out of their own data.
do: Bring five or six farms together on a **shared robot co-op**.
Put **twenty thousand** of my savings into the co-op.
Hire a **weeding robot** to test at Ridgeway.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but energised, like the night before harvest.
S3.quote: Small farmers should own the robots together, the way my grandparents' village shared one combine harvester.
fieldNote: With five years he shifts from defence to **building** something.
He's willing to risk a **large sum** because his cushion is strong.
He knows the local power broker is **Mr Hartley** and plans around him.

steps.text: Put twenty thousand into a robot co-op with local farms
Bring five local farms together to form the co-op
Hire a weeding robot for a trial at Ridgeway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole second career's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to train people properly, so every farmer should have a free course on robots and AI. I'd say it at the union and probably to the local paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think this one's good for me. Ten years is long enough to learn to build the farm robots instead of waiting to be replaced by one. I'd want to be the person designing them for small mixed farms like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd apply for a part-time robotics engineering degree at the university, about four years at evenings and weekends. I'd keep working at Ridgeway and keep doing the drone maps. And I'd put more into the index funds, since ten years is a long time for them to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Curious more than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not leave, just move up a level. I'd still want mud on my boots, just maybe fewer days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the people around you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo and Marek would need help more than me. Marek mostly drives, so in this picture Marek has ten years to retrain, and I'd nag him to start.

I'd tell the union and the **local paper** we have time to train people properly.
think: Privately this picture is **good for me** if I learn to build farm robots.
I'd aim at designing robots for **small mixed farms** like Ridgeway.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my favourite part of the job goes first and I'd have no time to build anything. What would help is public grants for farm co-ops to buy robots and a right-to-repair law. If a robot drives the tractor, I want the farmers and the workers to own the robot, not some company three countries away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about data. Every drone flight I make sends data to the drone company, and in an AGI world, whoever owns the data owns farming.

headlineQuote: If a robot drives the tractor, I want the farmers and the workers to own the robot, not some company three countries away.
portrait: Tomas is a 27-year-old **crop and tech lead** on a large arable and beef farm.
He's single, has **eighteen months saved** and index funds, and uses AI daily.
He's **pro-union** and wants farmers and workers to own robots together.
He is **calm** in mild pictures and **anxious** at AGI by 2028, since thinking AI hits his role first.
With time he plans a **robot co-op** and a robotics degree.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because his mapping job goes first with no time to build.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **public grants** for farm robot co-ops.
He wants a **right-to-repair** law for farm machines.
